lead: A piezoelectric crystal produces charge when squeezed and changes shape when a voltage is applied. This reversible pair is the direct and the inverse piezoelectric effect. The effect turns force, pressure and vibration into an electric signal without any external power, so the sensor is active. It also works backwards: the same crystal can push sound into air, water or metal. Quartz, PZT ceramics and PVDF film are the common materials. You meet these transducers in engine pressure measurement, vibration monitoring, medical scanners and ultrasonic distance sensors.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for dynamic characteristics and Unit 3 for capacitance and the parallel-plate formula C = ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub> A / t.

blocks.text: Press a quartz plate between two metal electrodes and charge appears on the electrodes. Remove the force and the charge falls back to zero. The charge reverses sign only if the force is reversed in direction, that is, if the plate is stretched instead of compressed. This is the direct piezoelectric effect: mechanical stress produces electric polarisation. Apply a voltage across the same plate and it becomes slightly thicker or thinner. This is the inverse effect: electric field produces strain. Both effects are linear and reversible for small signals, so one crystal can sense and also generate sound.

blocks.where: Q is the charge in coulombs (C); d is the charge coefficient in C/N, often quoted in pC/N; F is the applied force in newtons (N).

V is the open-circuit voltage in volts; g is the voltage coefficient in V·m/N, with g = d/ε; ε is the permittivity of the crystal, ε = ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub>, with ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m and ε<sub>r</sub> the relative permittivity (4.5 for quartz); t is the plate thickness in m; P is the pressure in N/m² (Pa). Some syllabi call g the voltage sensitivity.

items: Quartz: d = 2.3 pC/N and ε<sub>r</sub> ≈ 4.5. Very stable, low output, good for calibration.
PZT (lead zirconate titanate): d = 300–600 pC/N. High output, most common in sensors and ultrasound.
PVDF polymer film: d ≈ 20–30 pC/N. Thin, flexible, acoustic impedance close to water and tissue.

blocks.text: The coefficient depends on the crystal cut and on the direction of force. For poled ceramics and polymer films, a datasheet gives d<sub>33</sub> for force along the poling axis and d<sub>31</sub> for force at right angles to it; for quartz the quoted coefficient is d<sub>11</sub>.

sections.h3: Equivalent circuit and the steady-force problem

blocks.text: Electrically the crystal is a charge source q in parallel with its own capacitance C<sub>c</sub> and a leakage resistance R. For a plate of area A and thickness t, C<sub>c</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub> A / t, with ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m. R represents the crystal resistance plus insulator and cable leakage; for quartz it can exceed 10¹² Ω. The source is a charged capacitor, not a battery.

blocks.where: f<sub>L</sub> is the low-frequency cut-off in hertz; R is the leakage resistance in ohms; C<sub>c</sub> is the crystal capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: The charge leaks through R with time constant τ = R C<sub>c</sub>. A steady force therefore gives a voltage that decays to zero. Below f<sub>L</sub> the reading is wrong; above it the output follows the dynamic force. This is why piezoelectric sensors measure vibration, shock, pulses and cylinder pressure, not a weight sitting on a scale.

sections.h3: Signal conditioning: why a charge amplifier

blocks.text: A plain voltage amplifier measures V = q/(C<sub>c</sub> + C<sub>k</sub> + C<sub>in</sub>), where C<sub>k</sub> is cable capacitance and C<sub>in</sub> is amplifier input capacitance. Any change in cable length or position changes the gain, and a moving cable adds triboelectric noise.

A charge amplifier avoids this. The crystal connects to the virtual ground of an inverting op-amp, and a feedback capacitor C<sub>f</sub> carries the charge. The output is V<sub>out</sub> = −q/C<sub>f</sub>, independent of C<sub>c</sub>, C<sub>k</sub> and C<sub>in</sub>. A feedback resistor R<sub>f</sub> discharges C<sub>f</sub> and sets the low cut-off f<sub>L</sub> = 1/(2π R<sub>f</sub> C<sub>f</sub>).

blocks.where: V<sub>out</sub> is the amplifier output voltage in volts; q is the charge from the crystal in coulombs; C<sub>f</sub> is the feedback capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: After the charge amplifier a low-pass filter removes high-frequency noise, and the output goes to a recorder or ADC. For pressure, a diaphragm or a stack of crystal plates converts pressure to force. For a stack of n plates the charges add, so q = n d A P and Vout = −n d A P/Cf, with n = 1 for a single diaphragm. For ultrasound, a PZT element is driven by a short high-frequency burst and then listens for the echo. Echo timing and ranging are covered in Ultrasonic and acoustic sensors.

figure.caption: The crystal sends charge q into a high-impedance charge amplifier; the filter then cleans the voltage before output. Notice that the cable sits between crystal and charge amplifier, where cable capacitance no longer sets the gain.

spec.aria: A piezoelectric crystal feeds a charge amplifier, then a filter, then the output; the charge amplifier is the high-impedance block.

examples.question: A quartz disc has area 2 cm², thickness 1 mm, d = 2.3 pC/N and ε<sub>r</sub> = 4.5. A dynamic force of 10 N is applied along the sensitive axis. (a) Find the charge produced. (b) Find the crystal capacitance. (c) Find the open-circuit voltage. Take ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m.
steps: Convert area and thickness: A = 2 cm² = 2×10⁻⁴ m²; t = 1 mm = 1×10⁻³ m.
Charge: Q = d F = 2.3 pC/N × 10 N = 23 pC = 23×10⁻¹² C.
Capacitance: C<sub>c</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub> A / t = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m × 4.5 × 2×10⁻⁴ m² ÷ 1×10⁻³ m = 7.965×10⁻¹² F ≈ 7.97 pF.
Open-circuit voltage: V = Q / C<sub>c</sub> = 23×10⁻¹² C ÷ 7.965×10⁻¹² F = 2.89 V ≈ 2.9 V.
examples.answer: The charge is 23 pC, the crystal capacitance is 7.97 pF and the open-circuit voltage is 2.9 V.

A = 2e-4

traps: A piezoelectric sensor cannot measure a steady weight. The charge leaks away, so only a changing force gives a lasting output.
d is charge per newton (C/N or pC/N); g is voltage per unit stress (V·m/N). Do not mix the two coefficients.
Cable capacitance spoils a voltage amplifier but not a charge amplifier. Read the question: the answer changes with the circuit.
The unit pC/N means 10⁻¹² C/N. A d of 2.3 pC/N is not 2.3 C/N.
The crystal's sharp mechanical resonance is used for ultrasound, not for force measurement. A force sensor works well below resonance.

quiz.q: Define the direct and inverse piezoelectric effect. Name the coefficient d and give its unit.
quiz.a: Direct: stress produces charge. Inverse: voltage produces strain. d is the charge coefficient in C/N or pC/N.

quiz.q: Why does the output of a piezoelectric force sensor fall to zero under a constant load?
quiz.a: Charge leaks through the crystal and insulator resistance R with time constant τ = RC<sub>c</sub>. The sensor acts as a high-pass circuit with cut-off 1/(2πRC<sub>c</sub>).

quiz.q: Give two reasons a charge amplifier is preferred over a voltage amplifier for a piezoelectric sensor with a long cable.
quiz.a: Its output −q/C<sub>f</sub> does not depend on cable capacitance or crystal capacitance, and cable movement does not change the gain.

quiz.q: A PZT disc with d = 300 pC/N and capacitance 500 pF receives a dynamic force of 20 N. Find the charge and the open-circuit voltage.
A charge amplifier has C<sub>f</sub> = 100 pF and R<sub>f</sub> = 10 GΩ. Find the output for q = 50 pC and the low-frequency cut-off.
A quartz sensor has C<sub>c</sub> = 8 pF and leakage resistance 1 GΩ. Find the low-frequency cut-off. Will it measure a 0.5 Hz vibration?
quiz.a: f<sub>L</sub> = 1/(2π × 10⁹ Ω × 8×10⁻¹² F) = 19.9 Hz. The 0.5 Hz vibration is below cut-off, so the output is strongly attenuated and the sensor cannot measure it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers, or PMUTs, are built with MEMS processes for phone speakers and medical imaging. Piezoelectric energy harvesters convert footsteps or machine vibration into microwatts for wireless sensor nodes. Lead-free ceramics such as KNN are replacing PZT where toxicity matters. Structural health monitoring uses PVDF and PZT patches to listen for cracks in bridges and aircraft. Search: charge amplifier for piezoelectric sensor, d33 PZT, piezoelectric energy harvesting.
